results.title: Soil-water basics for irrigation scheduling
results.description: ### Soil-water basics for irrigation scheduling. Most of the irrigation in the state happens in the glacial outwash region where irrigation makes this region highly productive because of low water holding capacities and rapid drainage, however this is where most people depend on groundwater for their drinking water supply. Scheduling can be done by timely monitoring of the moisture content of the soil directly using soil moisture sensors, and indirectly by estimating crop water use of different crops (evapotranspiration) to model soil water depletion. A better understanding of the basic principles, definitions, and terms behind soil-water-plant relationship is fundamental and can aid communication between agricultural producers, extension educators, crop consultants, agency personnel and researchers. **Field capacity** – It is the amount of water that remains in the soil after all the excess water at saturation has been drained out. **Available water holding capacity (AWC)** –The amount of water that soil can store to be extracted by the plant.

results.description: This article compares two widely used soil water balance-based irrigation scheduling methods—Checkbook and FAO-56—by evaluating their principles, advantages, and limitations, with a focus on how each method tracks and manages soil moisture. results.title: Irrigation Scheduling Using Soil Water Tension Sensors - Alabama Cooperative Extension System
results.description: Soil sensors for irrigation scheduling. Soil water tension sensors are an effective tool in irrigation management, enabling producers to monitor soil water during the growing season and improve irrigation timing. The amount of water a soil can hold is influenced by many factors, such as soil texture and soil organic matter. Among the most used tools are soil water matric potential sensors, or soil water tension sensors (figure 1). These sensors deliver data that relate tension values to crop-available water. # Relationship Between Soil Water Tension and Soil Water Status. Soil water tension (SWT) is defined as the water pressure of a soil at a particular time, usually measured in kiloPascals (kPa) or centibars (cb). The saturation range goes from SWT of 0 kPa to SWT at field capacity. To achieve these efficiencies at this timing, the amount of irrigation to be applied should be calculated to bring soil water level back to field capacity (0 percent SWD).
